steps.title: Какие слова о человеке, а какие о задаче?
Четыре способа сказать, что человек смог
steps.html:
Only thirty per cent were able to resist the temptation. — способность была в той ситуации.

Some managed to wait a while. — было трудно, и всё же получилось.

Nearly all of them succeeded in waiting. — та же мысль, но после — форма на -ing.

The children who could not wait were less successful. — общая способность, в целом.

steps.title: В каком предложении понятно, что было трудно?
options: She could swim when she was five.
She managed to swim across the lake.
She was able to swim as a child.
steps.answer: She managed to swim across the lake.
steps.why: Manage to всегда несёт мысль о преодолённой трудности в конкретном случае.

steps.title: Какая форма и когда
steps.html:
ФормаКогда используемПример
can / can'tспособность сейчасI can wait when I have to.
could / couldn'tобщая способность в прошломAs a child I couldn't sit still.
was / were able toспособность в конкретной ситуации, прошлоеThirty per cent were able to resist.
managed toодин случай, и это было трудноSome managed to wait a while.
succeeded in + -ingодин случай, более формальноThey succeeded in waiting the full time.

steps.title: Как это работает
steps.html:
Для общей способности в прошлом обычно could: She could read at four.

Для конкретного случая, когда получилось, используют was able to или managed to, а не could.

В отрицании правило мягче: couldn't подходит в обоих случаях — I couldn't open the door.

Be able to нужна там, где у can формы нет: I'd like to be able to…, I've never been able to…, You'll be able to…

items.text: manage — Some children managed to wait a while before giving in.
resist — Only thirty per cent were able to resist temptation.
succeed — Nearly all the children succeeded in waiting the full fifteen minutes.
observe — The researchers observed the children through a camera.
avoid — The important thing was to avoid thinking about the marshmallow at all.

steps.title: Четырёхлетних оставляют наедине с конфетой на пятнадцать минут. Какого результата вы ждёте?
The marshmallow test
steps.html:
Прочитайте один раз. Главный — последний абзац.

In the late 1960s a professor at Stanford University sat four-year-old children down, one at a time, in a room with nothing in it but a table, a chair and a marshmallow. The rule was simple. You can eat this now. Or, if you can wait until I come back, you can have two. Then the researcher left, and a camera recorded what happened next.

Fifteen minutes is a long time when you are four. Nearly seventy per cent of the children ate the sweet. Some managed to wait a while before they gave in; others didn't last a minute. Only thirty per cent were able to resist the temptation for the full fifteen minutes. So far, the result was not very surprising.

The interesting part came years later. When the researchers contacted the same children as adults, the group who had waited were doing noticeably better: they had done well at school, they earned more, and they described healthier relationships. The children who could not wait were, on average, less successful in all of those ways. One marshmallow, it seemed, had measured something real.

But the experiment is often reported badly. It is not a test of who is born patient. When the team watched the film again, they noticed that the successful children were not fighting the marshmallow at all. Staring at it, picking it up or smelling it always ended the same way. The ones who succeeded in waiting looked away, covered their eyes, sang, or turned their chair around.

So Mischel tried teaching those techniques. He told a new group of children to imagine that the marshmallow was only a picture, not a real sweet. This time nearly all of them managed to wait. That is the finding worth keeping: the children who did best were not making a bigger effort than the others. They had simply found a way of not having to make one.

The children who could not wait were, on average, less successful in all of those ways. One marshmallow, it seemed, had measured something real.

But the experiment is often reported badly. It is not a test of who is born patient. When the team watched the film again, they noticed that the successful children were not fighting the marshmallow at all. Staring at it, picking it up or smelling it always ended the same way. The ones who succeeded in waiting looked away, covered their eyes, sang, or turned their chair around.

So Mischel tried teaching those techniques. He told a new group of children to imagine that the marshmallow was only a picture, not a real sweet. This time nearly all of them managed to wait. That is the finding worth keeping: the children who did best were not making a bigger effort than the others. They had simply found a way of not having to make one.

steps.title: Послушайте описание эксперимента. Что именно обещали ребёнку?
options: Два маршмеллоу, если дождётся возвращения исследователя
steps.answer: Два маршмеллоу, если дождётся возвращения исследователя
steps.html:
Прочитайте один раз. Главный — последний абзац.

In the late 1960s a professor at Stanford University sat four-year-old children down, one at a time, in a room with nothing in it but a table, a chair and a marshmallow. The rule was simple. You can eat this now. Or, if you can wait until I come back, you can have two. Then the researcher left, and a camera recorded what happened next.

Fifteen minutes is a long time when you are four. Nearly seventy per cent of the children ate the sweet. Some managed to wait a while before they gave in; others didn't last a minute. Only thirty per cent were able to resist the temptation for the full fifteen minutes. So far, the result was not very surprising.

The interesting part came years later. When the researchers contacted the same children as adults, the group who had waited were doing noticeably better: they had done well at school, they earned more, and they described healthier relationships. The children who could not wait were, on average, less successful in all of those ways. One marshmallow, it seemed, had measured something real.

But the experiment is often reported badly. It is not a test of who is born patient. When the team watched the film again, they noticed that the successful children were not fighting the marshmallow at all. Staring at it, picking it up or smelling it always ended the same way. The ones who succeeded in waiting looked away, covered their eyes, sang, or turned their chair around.

So Mischel tried teaching those techniques. He told a new group of children to imagine that the marshmallow was only a picture, not a real sweet. This time nearly all of them managed to wait. That is the finding worth keeping: the children who did best were not making a bigger effort than the others. They had simply found a way of not having to make one.

steps.title: Как говорить о том, что вам удаётся

items.text: I couldn't do it at first, but…
It took a lot of confidence to…

steps.title: Ответьте вслух.
items: Расскажите о трудности, с которой справились. Чем она была сложна?
Что вам так и не удаётся, как бы вы ни старались?
Сработала бы техника с маршмеллоу для взрослых? Почему?

steps.title: Теперь ответьте целиком одним высказыванием. Запишите себя.
steps.sub: Используйте managed to, was able to и couldn't хотя бы по разу.
items: The hardest thing I've had to do recently was … .
At first I couldn't … , but in the end I managed to … .
I've never been able to … , and I'm not sure I ever will.

steps.title: Урок 7 пройден
items: Я могу говорить о способностях, усилиях и успехе.
Я выбираю между could, was able to, managed to и succeeded in.
Я сохраняю правильные прошедшие формы, когда рассказываю.
Я вижу, чего описанный эксперимент не доказывает.
